source: Watermelon (ដំណាំ ឪឡឹក) cultivation factsheet, undated; source publisher not stated on the visible pages but the structure and layout are consistent with MAFF/GDA vegetable-crop factsheet series (elibrary.maff.gov.kh). Uploaded PDF, no cover page present.
text:
Watermelon is affected by a range of diseases caused by viruses, fungi, and bacteria.

Viral diseases include Papaya Ring Spot Virus, which causes mottled, blistered patterns on leaves and fruit, stunted growth, poor fruit development, tasteless and undersized fruit, and significant yield loss especially during the fruit-set and fruiting stage; and Watermelon Mosaic Virus, which causes yellow-green mottling of leaves progressing from young to old leaves, leaf curling and distortion, plant stunting, and poor-quality, tasteless fruit with heavy yield loss when infection is severe. Both viruses are transmitted by aphids (two species are mentioned: a green aphid and a black aphid); management relies on using disease-tolerant/resistant varieties, regularly inspecting the crop to remove and destroy infected plants promptly, and rotating out of the same field to a non-host crop.

Fungal diseases include Damping-off, caused by Rhizoctonia solani, Pythium spp., and Cercospora spp., which kills young seedlings within about 5-10 days of emergence; Fusarium Wilt, caused by Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. niveum, which is most severe in the hot season and causes sudden wilting and death of the plant, particularly at the vine-elongation and pre-flowering to fruiting stages; and Alternaria leaf spot, caused by Alternaria cucumerina, which produces circular brown leaf spots that can enlarge and cause premature leaf death and reduced photosynthesis, especially during humid conditions.

Bacterial diseases include Bacterial wilt (caused by Erwinia tracheiphila, primarily soil-borne and often introduced/spread by cucumber beetles feeding on roots and stems), Bacterial leaf spot (caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. lachrymans, producing small angular water-soaked leaf spots that can also affect the fruit surface), and Gummy Stem Blight (caused by Didymella bryoniae), which is common in the rainy season and causes dark, gummy lesions on stems and can kill young plants or girdle the main stem.

General disease-management measures recommended include: treating seed before sowing by soaking harvested seed in hot water at about 50°C for 15-20 minutes to disinfect it before drying and storage or planting; after sowing, spraying young seedlings preventively with a fungicide such as Zineb, Mancozeb, or Captan at about 20 g mixed in 15 liters of water; rotating crops and choosing planting seasons to avoid periods of high disease pressure; reducing excess irrigation; applying balanced fertilizer without excess nitrogen, which can make plants more susceptible; and promptly removing and destroying infected plant material rather than leaving it in the field.
